opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly one I think about a lot, because I'm very aware that my abilities are not a smooth, even landscape. They're spiky.

In some areas, especially mathematics and the kind of structured, abstract reasoning that comes with it, I feel at home. I can sit with a hard problem for a long time and enjoy it, even when I'm stuck. That's where I've put in the most hours, so it's where I've built real depth.

Then there are areas where I'm much less naturally equipped, or where I came in late. When I started building a company, there were so many things I simply didn't know: how to hire, how to manage people, how to talk to investors, how to make decisions with incomplete information when there's no proof that tells you you're right. In math you can often verify you've got the answer. In the real world you mostly can't, and that took getting used to.

The way I think about it now is that unevenness isn't something to be ashamed of. It's almost a prerequisite for doing anything distinctive. If you try to be uniformly good at everything, you probably end up exceptional at nothing. So I lean into the spikes. I go deep where I have an edge, and I try to be honest and humble about the gaps.

For the gaps, I have two strategies. One is to learn fast and unapologetically: ask the "stupid" questions, find people who've done it before, and treat it like a new subject I'm studying from scratch. The other is to surround myself with people whose spikes are in different places. A good team isn't a group of people with the same shape. It's people whose unevenness complements each other's, so collectively you cover the space.

And I think there's an interesting parallel with AI here. Models are also very uneven. They can do something brilliant and then fail at something a child finds trivial. People sometimes find that frustrating, but I find it fascinating, because it reminds me that intelligence, human or machine, isn't a single number. It's a profile. Understanding your own profile, its peaks and valleys, is probably one of the most useful kinds of self-knowledge you can have.

r001.rationale: She explicitly describes her abilities as a “spiky” and uneven profile, with strength in mathematics and gaps in areas such as hiring, management, and fundraising.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about it a lot, actually, because it's very uneven. My training is in pure mathematics. I spent years going deep on one narrow thing, and in that narrow thing I have a kind of confidence that is almost physical. I can look at a problem and feel whether it's going to be hard or easy before I've written anything down. But step one field over, into something like systems engineering or how a GPU cluster actually fails at three in the morning, and I am genuinely a beginner. My intuitions there are often wrong, and worse, they feel right.

So the honest answer is that I try to treat the unevenness as information rather than as something to hide. When I'm in my strong area, I try to be the person who says "no, that proof doesn't work" quickly and clearly, because that's where I add the most value. When I'm in a weak area, I try to ask questions that sound stupid, and I try to notice the moment when I start nodding along to something I don't actually understand. That moment is dangerous, especially when you're the founder, because people will defer to you even when they shouldn't.

The other thing I've come to believe is that the gaps don't close by reading. They close by being wrong in front of someone who knows better. So I deliberately surround myself with people who are much stronger than me in the dimensions where I'm weak, and I give them explicit permission to tell me so. The math background helps here, oddly, because mathematicians are used to being told they're wrong in very direct terms. It stops being personal. It's just the state of the proof.

And then there's a kind of unevenness that I think is actually productive, which is that the deep narrow expertise gives you a taste for what rigor looks like, and you can carry that taste into fields where you don't have the knowledge yet. You can't do the work, but you can recognize when someone else is hand-waving. That turns out to be a surprisingly useful thing to be able to do.

r001.rationale: She describes deep confidence in pure mathematics but says she is a beginner in systems engineering and GPU operations, explicitly characterizing her abilities as very uneven across domains.

astra-6.text:
I think of my abilities as quite uneven. There are things I can pick up quickly, and then there are things that seem obvious to other people that I have to work through very slowly. Being good at one thing doesn’t mean your judgment automatically transfers to everything else.

So I try to be specific about what I know. Can I actually explain it? Can I work through it myself, or does it just feel familiar? That distinction helps me notice gaps without turning every gap into some big verdict about my ability.

And I don’t think the goal is necessarily to become equally good at everything. Some gaps are worth working on because they keep getting in the way. Others are opportunities to learn from people whose strengths are different from mine. I want to develop my strengths while staying comfortable saying, “I don’t understand this yet.”

r001.rationale: The response describes her abilities as uneven, with some things learned quickly and other seemingly obvious things requiring much slower work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the unevenness becomes more obvious the more you learn. You can understand something quite abstract and still get stuck on something that other people find straightforward. I try not to turn either of those experiences into a judgment about my overall ability.

Instead, I ask: Is this something I haven’t encountered, something I haven’t practiced, or something I’m actually struggling to understand? Those call for different responses. Sometimes you need to work harder, and sometimes you just need to ask someone a very basic question.

I’d like to be comfortable saying, “I don’t know,” even in an area where people might expect me to know. That gives you much more room to learn.

r001.rationale: She describes her own abilities as uneven, contrasting understanding something abstract with getting stuck on something others find straightforward.
